title: Udaipur's Ganesh Emporium Turns Antique Textiles Into a Travel Destination
excerpt: In a restored 17th-century haveli, designer Vipul Shah's family has turned a 1980s textile shop into one of Udaipur's most-visited cultural stops — where shoppers come for the stories as much as the bags.
body:
• Ganesh Emporium began in 1980 as a 100-square-foot shop founded by Vipul Shah's parents and uncles after the family moved from Ahmedabad to Udaipur; it now occupies a restored 17th-century haveli with 65 galleries.
  • The emporium houses antique textiles, vintage Pichwais, miniature paintings and artefacts gathered by the family over decades, and travellers increasingly plan their Udaipur days around a visit.
  • Shah's bag line uses vintage fabrics — wedding textiles, dowry embroidery, tribal costumes — so each piece carries a history that predates the purchase; online listings range from about Rs 6,000 for clutches to Rs 20,000 for larger styles.
  • Practically: it sits on City Palace Road in the old city, is open roughly 9:30 am to 7:30 pm, and pairs naturally with the City Palace and a sunset boat ride on Lake Pichola.

Udaipur is a city of planned itineraries abandoned every few minutes — a carved doorway, an old balcony, a lake view that makes you forget you were supposed to be somewhere else. On City Palace Road, one stop has quietly joined the must-visit list: Ganesh Emporium, a 65-gallery emporium inside a restored 17th-century haveli where shopping has become a cultural experience built on antique textiles, craftsmanship and stories.

Opening lead: the building is part of the experience

Visitors walk through carved stone windows, old balconies and winding staircases, past galleries of vintage Pichwais, antique textiles, miniature paintings and old artefacts collected over many years. "I don't think it happened overnight. It happened quietly over the years. People weren't just coming to shop anymore. They were coming to experience the place itself," Vipul Shah, founder of Vipul Shah Bags and part of the family behind the emporium, told HT Travel.

Context & Background: three generations of collecting

Ganesh Emporium began in 1980 as a tiny 100-square-foot shop after Shah's parents and uncles moved from Ahmedabad to Udaipur. Each generation added something: textile preservation, art collecting, haveli restoration, and new ideas from the younger generation. When Vipul joined the family business after graduating, he began looking at the family's antique textile collection differently — those fabrics became the foundation for his bag line.

Some of the textiles used in the bags have histories of their own: wedding textiles, dowry embroidery, tribal costumes. The material had already lived a life before it became part of a handbag. Robb Report India, which profiled Shah earlier this year, called the emporium "a living, breathing museum of Indian artistry."

"When my father and his brothers began Ganesh Emporium in the early 1980's, their vision was rooted in simplicity — bringing India's finest crafts to a world that was just discovering Udaipur," Shah told Robb Report India. "Today, its purpose has moved beyond commerce. It has become a living archive, a sanctuary for textiles, and a space where history and craftsmanship unfold room by room."

Impact & Analysis: travellers plan trips around it

Shah first realised the emporium had become more than a shopping stop when people began contacting the family before even planning the rest of their Udaipur trip. "They weren't asking what to buy. They were asking when they could spend time at the haveli," he said.

"If someone takes home a Vipul Shah bag, I hope they're also taking home a little piece of Udaipur. Its craftsmanship, its warmth, and the feeling of discovering the city beyond the obvious."

— Vipul Shah, Founder, Vipul Shah Bags

The visit rewards a slow pace: give yourself at least an hour or two to explore the galleries and ask about the textiles. "The haveli reflects the city," Shah told HT Travel, and visitors frequently tell him they saw a different side of Udaipur because of their visit.

A diaspora note: a souvenir with a lineage

For diaspora travellers visiting Rajasthan, the emporium offers something increasingly rare: a souvenir with a documented past. The vintage textiles — wedding fabrics, dowry embroidery, tribal costumes — are rooted in craft traditions rather than manufactured for the tourist market, and many visitors return with friends and family.

What's Next: planning your visit

Shah's ideal Udaipur day starts with an early morning hike in the Aravalli hills, then a walk through the old city's lanes, temples and flower and spice markets. Ganesh Emporium pairs naturally with the nearby City Palace; by evening, he recommends a sunset boat ride on Lake Pichola. For food, his advice is simple: kachori and gulab jamun, eaten warm.

Practically, the emporium is on City Palace Road in the old city — best reached by auto-rickshaw, given the narrow lanes — and is open roughly 9:30 am to 7:30 pm, though timings should be confirmed. Current online listings put bags between about Rs 6,000 and Rs 20,000. Prices and opening hours are indicative and should be confirmed with the emporium before visiting.
image_caption: Handbags from the Vipul Shah line, fashioned from vintage Rajasthani textiles. The bags are sold at Ganesh Emporium in Udaipur, the family-run, 65-gallery emporium housed in a restored 17th-century haveli.
